title: Busy Beaver \(\mathrm{BB}(6)\)
formal:
Determine the exact six-state binary Busy Beaver runtime \(\mathrm{BB}(6)=S(6)\) by giving a concrete machine \(M_*\in\mathcal M_6\) and proving
\[M_*\text{ halts on the blank tape},\qquad
\forall M\in\mathcal M_6:\ M\text{ halts on the blank tape}\ \Longrightarrow\ T(M)\le T(M_*).\]
Here \(\mathcal M_6\) is the finite class of deterministic six-nonhalting-state, two-symbol Turing machines defined below, and \(T(M)\) is the number of transitions through the first entry into the separate halting state. The complete transition table of \(M_*\), together with proofs of its halting and universal maximality, specifies the answer exactly as \(S(6)=T(M_*)\).
definitions:
Machine. Fix the nonhalting states \(Q=\{A,B,C,D,E,F\}\), one additional halting state \(Z\notin Q\), and the tape alphabet \(\{0,1\}\). A machine is a total transition function
\[\delta:Q\times\{0,1\}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}\times\{-1,+1\}\times(Q\cup\{Z\}).\]
Thus its description has exactly twelve entries. The three outputs specify the symbol to write, a move of exactly one cell left or right, and the next state, respectively. There are no stationary moves, extra tapes or transitions out of \(Z\). Unreachable states and entries are allowed. Different tables need not have different behavior; no symmetry reduction is imposed on the quantified class \(\mathcal M_6\).

Execution. The tape is indexed by all integers. A configuration consists of a state \(q\), a head position \(h\in\mathbb Z\), and a tape function \(\tau:\mathbb Z\to\{0,1\}\). At time zero, \(q=A\), \(h=0\), and \(\tau(i)=0\) for every integer \(i\). If \(q\ne Z\) and \(\delta(q,\tau(h))=(b,d,q')\), one transition replaces \(\tau(h)\) by \(b\), leaves every other tape cell unchanged, replaces the head position by \(h+d\), and enters \(q'\). Execution stops immediately on entering \(Z\); that final write-and-move transition is included in the count. Each transition costs one step, irrespective of head position or time elapsed. There is no external input, randomness or resource limit.

Halting time and maximum. A machine halts if its unique execution first enters \(Z\) at some positive integer time. Only for such a machine, \(T(M)\) denotes this least time. Let \(\mathcal H_6\subseteq\mathcal M_6\) be the halting machines. Define
\[S(6)=\max\{T(M):M\in\mathcal H_6\}.\]
There are \(28^{12}\) tables in \(\mathcal M_6\), since each entry has \(2\cdot2\cdot7\) choices. The halting subset is nonempty, since a table can send \((A,0)\) directly to \(Z\). Hence the maximum exists as a finite positive integer. No value of \(T\) on a nonhalting machine is used in the statement or the submitted certificate.

Answer representation. The runtime of a specified, proved-halting table defines an exact integer through a terminating step-counting computation, even when actually evaluating it is infeasible. The accepted answer need not separately evaluate that computation. In this card, \(\mathrm{BB}\) always means the runtime maximum \(S\), not the distinct extremal function \(\Sigma\) that maximizes the number of ones on the final tape.

Notation in the context. For positive integer \(k\), \(2\uparrow\uparrow k\) is a tower of \(k\) twos, equivalently \(2\uparrow\uparrow1=2\) and \(2\uparrow\uparrow(k+1)=2^{(2\uparrow\uparrow k)}\). Three arrows mean iteration of this tower operation: \(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow1=2\) and \(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow(k+1)=2\uparrow\uparrow(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow k)\).
answer_criterion:
Supply the complete twelve-entry transition table of a particular \(M_*\in\mathcal M_6\), with complete mathematically correct proofs checked in Lean that it halts from the stated blank initial configuration and that every halting \(M\in\mathcal M_6\) has \(T(M)\le T(M_*)\). These two proofs must establish the exact equality \(\mathrm{BB}(6)=T(M_*)\). This is the user-approved exact witness criterion, superseding the default numerical tolerance for this card only.

The witness runtime is an accepted exact finite description of the integer. A simple closed form, decimal expansion, separately evaluated integer literal or full execution trace is not required. A candidate machine without both proofs, an estimated runtime, a one-sided bound, a list of undecided machines or a restatement of the defining maximum is insufficient. Any reduction to representative transition tables must itself be justified as covering the full stated class. A result for a different alphabet, state count, tape convention or final-tape score does not settle this target.
why: The halting behavior of a finite set of exceptionally short programs is still beyond complete classification. This problem makes the boundary of current computability knowledge concrete: one additional nonhalting state separates the established five-state maximum from an unresolved maximum with enormous certified examples and difficult residual halting questions. A solution would give a universal exact upper bound for every halting program in this precisely fixed class.

importance.reason: A landmark finite problem at the frontier of computability and formal verification, asking for the next binary Busy Beaver runtime value after the resolved five-state case.

context_blocks.text: Radó introduced Busy Beaver functions in 1962 as concrete examples of noncomputability. The runtime function takes a maximum over finitely many halting programs at each state count, but there is no algorithm computing all its values. That statement about the entire sequence does not make every individual value unknowable. The first five binary runtime values have now been determined.

Finiteness alone does not supply an effective stopping rule for the search: a machine still running may halt much later or may run forever. Conversely, a proved value of \(S(6)\) would decide blank-tape halting for every table in this finite class in principle, by checking whether it halts within that many steps. The enormous possible duration makes this a mathematical consequence, not a practical promise.

The collaboration proves \(S(5)=47{,}176{,}870\) in Coq, now called Rocq. Its 2026 revised paper proves coverage of the relevant five-state machines as well as their halting classifications. The total number of representatives examined by that proof is \(181{,}385{,}789\); it is not a count of six-state holdouts or of all syntactically distinct tables in this card.

The formal paper presents halting entries as undefined transitions. Its convention counts the final attempt to execute such an entry, so even an immediately halting machine takes one step. Replacing an undefined entry by a write/move transition into the separate state Z preserves its runtime exactly. The card retains total twelve-entry tables to make a submitted witness fully explicit.

For six states, the paper records the lower bound \(S(6)>2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow5\). Appendix B carefully separates two kinds of evidence: the champion’s halting is proved in Coq, while the stated enormous step lower bound is estimated mathematically from its verified abstract evolution rules. The paper does not claim a formally verified exact runtime for that champion or a proof of universal six-state maximality.

Runtime and final output are different objectives. The function \(\Sigma(n)\) maximizes the number of ones present when a machine halts; \(S(n)\) maximizes the duration. Even their maximizing machines need not coincide: the paper records this already for three states. Approximate final-output formulas in a champion table therefore cannot simply be used as an exact answer for runtime.

One unresolved six-state behavior is Antihydra. Its halting question has an equivalent arithmetic form: start at \(a_0=8\) and iterate \(a_{j+1}=\lfloor3a_j/2\rfloor\). It halts exactly when some finite prefix of \(a_0,a_1,\ldots\) contains strictly more than twice as many odd terms as even terms. This is a particular recurrence question; resemblance to the classical Collatz problem is not an equivalence with that conjecture.

The Antihydra page discusses a probabilistic model suggesting nonhalting. The machine itself is deterministic, and a heuristic probability is not a halting or nonhalting proof. More generally, the six-state project distinguishes proved halters from unresolved machines, including examples heuristically expected to halt. Those expectations cannot certify a Busy Beaver upper bound.

The holdout table records 964 remaining six-state representatives in the entry dated 8 September 2026, attributed to mxdys. Some equivalent machines are omitted. The page warns that contributed lists are not uniformly independently verified, and this particular entry does not yet link a downloadable list. The number is therefore a dated project progress report, not a checked exhaustion theorem.

Holdout counts need not decrease monotonically: when an incompletely specified representative reaches a previously undefined transition, further completions of its table may need to be considered. Counts also depend on which equivalences have been removed. A smaller list measures progress in classification but is neither the Busy Beaver value nor a substitute for a universal proof.

The accepted answer isolates exactly what must be established: one explicit halting machine attaining the maximum, with a proof that every halting machine in the stated class takes no more steps. It can name an integer far beyond feasible decimal expansion through that certified runtime. Neither the general noncomputability theorem nor speculation about axiomatic independence supplies this requested witness.
